content:
In a new study, Apple researchers detail SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model capable of generating protein sequences and structures simultaneously. Details below.

Some background

Last September, Apple researchers published a study titled "SimpleFold: Folding Proteins Is Simpler Than You Think," detailing a streamlined method for predicting 3D protein structures from amino acid sequences.

In short, SimpleFold uses flow matching models to directly generate 3D protein structures from amino acid sequences.

We've explained flow matching in detail before, but in brief, the technique starts from a noisy random point and learns a relatively direct path to the final result. This is in contrast to diffusion models, which typically reach their final output through iterative denoising.

The most common (or at least historically most common) application of both techniques has been image generation, though researchers (including those at Apple) have also explored using diffusion models for text and code generation.

Returning to SimpleFold, Apple essentially combined flow matching with general-purpose Transformer blocks (typically used for text generation), allowing the model to bypass some of the more computationally intensive techniques found in traditional protein folding models (such as DeepMind's well-known AlphaFold).

Now, Apple researchers have introduced SimpleDesign, applying the simpler, more general-purpose architectural concepts explored in SimpleFold to the broader problem of protein design—not just predicting 3D protein structures.

SimpleDesign

As Apple researchers explain in a new study titled "SimpleDesign: A Unified Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Co-design":

In other words, while many existing protein design models rely on multi-stage pipelines, SimpleDesign learns to simultaneously generate amino acid sequences and continuous 3D structures in a single, end-to-end training process.

Many existing co-design models work like this: first, they train a separate model to convert protein structures into discrete representations, or "tokens." Then, they train a generative model to manipulate these representations, thereby producing new protein sequences and structures.

SimpleDesign skips this intermediate step; rather than first compressing protein structures into separate tokenized representations, it learns directly from paired amino acid sequences and 3D coordinates.

The Apple researchers used a rather interesting approach to train SimpleDesign.

They started with a dataset containing over 2 million pairs of protein sequences and structures, primarily from the AFESM dataset, which combines predicted structures from the AlphaFold database along with other samples.

During training, they perturbed both parts of each pair: amino acids in the sequence were randomly masked with mask tokens, while noise was added to the corresponding 3D structure.

The researchers also varied the degree of perturbation on both sides. If the sequence was largely intact but the structure was heavily corrupted, the task became similar to protein folding, requiring the model to recover the structure from the known sequence.

Conversely, if the structure was largely intact but the sequence was heavily masked, it was like inverse folding—the model had to generate a sequence capable of producing the specified structure.

When both were partially perturbed, the model had to learn to handle both problems simultaneously, effectively training for protein co-design.

According to the study, SimpleDesign achieved competitive results on benchmarks for protein co-design, structure generation, and sequence generation, despite a notably simpler training pipeline.

The researchers also found that SimpleDesign could generate plausible protein structures, and the amino acid sequences it produced were roughly on par with most competing multimodal models, and in some cases even better.

Finally, the researchers noted that SimpleDesign's results are currently limited to computational evaluations, as the generated proteins have not yet been experimentally tested to confirm that they can actually fold, function, or operate safely in real biological systems.

However, these results are quite encouraging, and the full study (which, of course, delves deeper into SimpleDesign's architecture, training process, benchmarks, and results) is well worth reading.
